title: FULL LECTURE: Professor John Mearsheimer Explains Why the US and China Are Inevitably Headed for War
summary: A lecture by a realist scholar arguing that anarchy and the drive to survive push great powers into rivalry, so a rising China and the US are bound to compete despite trade.

assertions.quote: I was making the argument that China cannot rise peacefully
when those economic theories or economic interdependence theory clashes with realist logic, realist logic will win almost every time.
Do you seriously think the Russians are going to tolerate us moving right up to their border?
it's going to want to dominate East Asia the way we dominate the Western Hemisphere

verdicts.note: China's build-up and pressure on its neighbours fit a bid for regional primacy, but its ultimate aims are a matter of intent that public records only partly show.

assertions.quote: the United States should not facilitate China's rise. It was a huge mistake. You're going to create a peer competitor.

verdicts.note: Trade and WTO entry sped China's growth, which funds its military, though its rise owed most to its own reforms.

assertions.quote: I believe that World War I was basically a preventive war started by Germany

verdicts.note: The Fischer school and others see German fear of a rising Russia as decisive, but many historians spread responsibility across several powers.

The case file says many German leaders favoured a preventive war against a rising Russia, Berlin gave Vienna its 'blank check', and Germany declared war on Russia and France. It also says blame is endlessly debated and that two rivalries turned a regional Austro-Serbian war into the world war.

assertions.quote: I think that realism provides the best explanation for how the world works.

verdicts.note: Which theory of international relations explains most is a scholarly judgment with no agreed test.

Clauset's finding that interstate war statistics look stationary supports realism's stationary null over liberal claims of a trend to peace, but it concerns aggregate war statistics, not great-power behaviour generally.
Cunen et al. reject the stationarity that realist accounts rely on, finding war sizes fell after about 1950, with democracy increasingly pacifying, which fits liberal mechanisms.
